A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the paleogeographic distribution of warm and cold water carbonate platforms in the late Paleozoic was controlled by the latitudinal distribution of warm and cool surface waters, respectively, which in turn was controlled by the geographic distribution of the high-latitude ice sheets.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the paleogeographic location of a marine carbonate platform is not the only control on the nature of the carbonate facies that form there; the paleoclimatic setting is also important.

the climate models used here are capable of simulating the paleoceanographic and paleoclimatic patterns recorded in the Upper Pennsylvannian – Lower Permian marine sediments of the Paleo-Tetthys Ocean.
oceanic circulation can be an important driver of marine biotic distribution, diversity, abundance, and ecosystem evolution.
